note: The outreach standard v3 (28 Sep 2026, signed by Benny-san), from ops/design/2026-09-28-relay-messaging-audit/outreach-standard.md. The same for every campaign: campaign specifics come from the research pack, the lookup and the campaign's industries. The rules and exemplars go to the writer; the tell list goes to the writer as a list and gives advice on the card, never a hold. The exemplars are the standard's worked sequence with a made-up person and firm of the same kind, and the rep's two approved messages as vendored in agents/outreach/voice/anchors.json.
rules: Written by the rep, to one person. Continue the rep's own messages (`voice`): plain words and contractions, soft hedges ("I'd guess", "I reckon", "curious"), openers that drop the "I" ("Saw…", "Been…"), a little loose, never sanded into even, polished prose. British English. No em dashes, exclamation marks, bullets, links or emoji. Short: people read on their phones.

About them, not us. The hook is one real, specific thing about their firm or role, from the lookup or the plan, said with curiosity. Write to the role: runs it, the working day; champions it, what they would need to show; signs it off, the outcome and the risk in the fewest words. If another firm's name would still fit, rewrite it about this firm.
One ask per touch, about interest, never a time, a meeting length or a calendar link. The connection note and the last email may end on a statement.

No pitch in Email 1. It may carry one light true line about the rep, "I've been helping a few <kind of firm> get a proper look at calls like that", naming the kind of firm from the campaign's industries. The product appears once in the sequence, in one plain sentence in Email 2 or the LinkedIn follow-up, tied to the problem and citing its live facts. Price only in the call script's answer to a price question, complete, from the price facts.

Evidence is optional. When a source fits, use a short exact fragment of its words from `pack.evidence`, inside your own plain sentence, and name the source in that sentence. Each item at most once in a sequence, and never one a colleague at the same firm was sent.

Never invent. No firm, person, number, line of business, event, experience, customer or result that is not in the lookup, the pack or the facts. The firm's line of business is the lookup's `lines`, or the campaign's industries. Their name or "they", never a gender guess. Never the name of the tool that drafts these messages.
Colleagues: up to three people per firm, one per buyer role. Each gets their own angle, hook and evidence, written to their role. They never receive the same email.

The limits. Email 1 50 to 100 words, subject 2 to 4 plain words. Connection note at most 200 characters. LinkedIn message 40 to 70 words, one breath, and it may open "Thanks for connecting". Email 2 at most 90 words and the last email at most 50, both replies in Email 1's thread. LinkedIn follow-up at most 50 words. Each call has its own opener and one question, and a voicemail under 40 words. Write the body only: the greeting and the sign-off are added.

exemplars.shows: Email 1 · champions it · opens on a firm fact from the lookup (its own complaints report), said with curiosity · the one light line about the rep, naming the kind of firm · one genuine question about how they handle it today · no product

draft.subject: your three-day number
draft.body:
Saw Hollin Cover's complaints report for the first half of the year, 25% closed within three days. I'd guess a fair few of the rest are the ones where someone has to go back and work out what actually got said on the call.

I've been helping a few insurers get a proper look at calls like that. Curious how your team gets to the bottom of those ones at the moment?
draft.ask: Curious how your team gets to the bottom of those ones at the moment?

exemplars.shows: The connection note · who and why in one breath · no pitch and no problem · ends on a statement

draft.body: Hi Jo, sent you a note about complaints at Hollin Cover. Would be good to connect.

exemplars.shows: The call script · each call its own opener and one question · a short voicemail with no pressure · the price answer complete, from the price facts, and only there

talkingPoint.openingLine: Hi Jo, it's Sam from Conversant. I emailed on Monday about complaints at Hollin Cover, have I caught you at a bad time?
talkingPoint.oneQuestion: When a complaint needs digging into, how do you get back to what was actually said on the call?
talkingPoint.openingLine2: Hi Jo, Sam from Conversant again, I sent a couple of emails about complaints, is now any better?
talkingPoint.oneQuestion2: When you're working out why a complaint happened, who else gets pulled in?
talkingPoint.listenFor: Whether getting back to what was said on a call is slow or guesswork today, and whether Jo owns fixing that or knows who does.
talkingPoint.voicemail: Hi Jo, Sam from Conversant. Dropped you an email about complaints, no need to call back, I'll try you again next week.

objections.answer: It's £4.99, £7.99 or £9.99 per seat a month depending on the plan, month to month, plus a one-off £1,280 setup and a £640 configuration review around month one.

exemplars.shows: Email 2 · a reply in the thread with a new angle, not a reminder · a short exact fragment of the evidence with its source named in the sentence · the sequence's one plain product sentence, citing one live fact · an interest ask

draft.body:
One other thing I was thinking about. When the FCA looked at root cause work across 40 firms, one of its points was that firms "did not always measure the impact" of the changes they made. I'd imagine that's the hard bit, knowing whether a fix actually stuck.

That's mostly what we built Insights360 for, it scores every call against your own QA rules so you can see whether something changed. Worth a chat?

exemplars.shows: The LinkedIn message after they accept · opens on thanks for connecting · a new angle on their world in one breath · a question · no product and no offer

draft.body: Thanks for connecting Jo. With home and motor under one roof I'd imagine complaints come in waves, storm claims one month, renewals the next. Does your team feel that swing much, or is it fairly steady right through the year?
draft.ask: Does your team feel that swing much, or is it fairly steady right through the year?

exemplars.shows: The LinkedIn follow-up · light and easy to ignore · offers something useful the thread has already raised · ends on a statement

draft.body: No worries if now's not the time Jo. If it'd help I can send over the FCA's write-up on root cause work, it's a decent read.
draft.ask: If it'd help I can send over the FCA's write-up on root cause work, it's a decent read.

exemplars.shows: The last email · a reply in the thread · closes the loop warmly with the right-person close · no guilt

draft.body: I'll leave it here so I'm not cluttering your inbox. If this sits with someone else at Hollin Cover, happy to be pointed their way.
draft.ask: If this sits with someone else at Hollin Cover, happy to be pointed their way.

exemplars.shows: The rep's own approved cold email (the voice anchor): runs it · curiosity about a real swing in their world · the light line about the rep · a mid-body question and a real question to close

draft.subject: when the season turns
draft.body:
Saw you run the contact centre at Throttle Cover. Spring must be brutal, everyone back on the bikes at once and the accident calls stacking up while the team goes from quiet to flat-out in a fortnight.

I've been helping a few insurers get a proper look at calls like that. Mostly though I'm just curious how a seasonal operation copes with that swing, do you flex the team or lean on the people who've been through it before?

How do you handle it when the season turns?
draft.ask: How do you handle it when the season turns?

exemplars.shows: The rep's own approved LinkedIn message (the voice anchor): one breath, why they reached out, one plain context line and a question · no offer
